title: Why we sleep on it
text: Students who pull all-nighters before exams suspect, correctly, that they are making a mistake. Sleep is not the absence of learning but part of it: during deep sleep the brain {{1}} the day's experiences, shifting fragile memories into more permanent storage. Experiments show that people who sleep after studying remember measurably more than those who remain {{2}}, even when the total amount of study time is identical. Sleep also tidies: the brain replays important episodes, prunes the trivial and {{3}} new learning to old knowledge, which is partly why insights so often arrive at breakfast. The effect works both ways. A tired brain not only stores less; it also exaggerates the emotional {{4}} of bad events, which is why worries feel heaviest at three in the morning. Nor is the benefit confined to full nights: a short afternoon nap can {{5}} for a short night, provided it lasts long enough to {{6}} deep sleep. The practical advice for learners is therefore {{7}}: review the difficult material in the evening, then {{8}} the temptation to revise until dawn. The extra page crammed at midnight is worth far less than the sleep that follows it.

gaps.explanation: 'consolidates the day's experiences' — makes them firm and permanent; condense (compress), conserve (save) and convene (meet) are form traps.
'remain awake' = stay out of sleep; alert and aware describe attention, and asleep would reverse the comparison.
'attaches new learning to old knowledge' — links it on; attract, attack and attend are near-form traps.
'the emotional impact of bad events' — the force of their effect; impulse = sudden urge, input = contribution, intake = amount consumed.
'a nap can compensate for a short night' — make up for the loss; compete for = contest, comply takes 'with', collude = conspire.
'long enough to reach deep sleep' — arrive at that stage; 'arrive' needs 'at', approach means get near without entering, obtain is not used with sleep stages.
'the advice is straightforward' — simple and easy to follow; the context describes easy steps, which rules out the other three.
'resist the temptation' — hold out against it; assist = help, insist takes 'on', persist takes 'in'.
